actions.name: conducted computer network exploitation (CNE) operations originating from China
actions.description: The actors, Zhang Haoran and Tan Dailin, collaborated with Chengdu 404 Network Technology company employees Qian Chuan, Fu Qiang, and Jiang Lizhi to conduct computer network exploitation (CNE) operations originating from China.

actions.name: used spearphishing emails with malicious files to gain initial access
actions.description: The group uses a wide range of tactics in order to gain Initial Access. Spearphishing emails with malicious files is a common tactic for the actors.

actions.name: targeted HR departments with malicious archive files masqueraded as applicant resumes
actions.description: Spearphishing themes frequently target HR departments with malicious archive files masqueraded as applicant resumes.

actions.name: used Microsoft Compiled HTML Help (CHM) files within spearphishing messages
actions.description: The group historically used Microsoft Compiled HTML Help (CHM) files within their spearphishing messages.

actions.name: conducted supply chain compromises resulting in victimization of third-party customers
actions.description: The group conducted supply chain compromises resulting in the victimization of third-party customers throughout the world.

actions.name: obtained login credentials belonging to individuals with administrative access to victim networks
actions.description: These actors typically obtain means of identification, such as login credentials belonging to individuals with administrative access to victim computer networks, to expand their unauthorized access.

actions.name: deployed legitimate third-party VPN software such as SoftEther on victim networks
actions.description: The actors may deploy legitimate third-party VPN software such as SoftEther on victim networks to facilitate follow-on access to the victim network.

actions.name: deployed “Skeleton Key” malware to create a master password for any account in the domain
actions.description: The group has also deployed “Skeleton Key” malware to create a master password that will work for any account in the domain.

actions.name: conducted a massive campaign to rapidly exploit publicly identified security vulnerabilities
actions.description: During early 2020, the group conducted a massive campaign to rapidly exploit publicly identified security vulnerabilities.

actions.name: gained access into victim accounts using publicly available exploit code against VPN services or public facing applications
actions.description: This technique allowed the group to gain access into victim accounts using publicly available exploit code against VPN services or public facing applications without using their own distinctive or identifying malware.

actions.name: installed widely available remote access tools like Cobalt Strike after exploiting vulnerabilities
actions.description: These compromises typically resulted in the installation of widely available remote access tools like Cobalt Strike.

actions.name: used malware families including gh0st, 9002, Zxshell, HK Door, XSLCMD, PlugX/Sogu, Derusbi, HiKit, Crosswalk/ProxIP, Winnti/Pasteboy/Stone/Treadstone, Azazel, PoisonPlug/Barlaiy/ShadowPad, metasploit-meterpreter, and Cobalt Strike
actions.description: The group has used the following malware: gh0st, 9002, Zxshell, HK Door, XSLCMD, PlugX/Sogu, Derusbi, HiKit, Crosswalk/ProxIP, Winnti/Pasteboy/Stone/Treadstone, Azazel, PoisonPlug/Barlaiy/ShadowPad, metasploit-meterpreter, and Cobalt Strike.

actions.name: used numerous webshells including China Chopper
actions.description: The group also uses numerous webshells including China Chopper.

actions.name: used DLL side-loading for persistence by implanting malware in loadperf.dll and winmm.dll
actions.description: One common persistence technique the group has used is DLL side-loading. The group frequently implanted malware in “%WINDIR%\Windows\System32\wbem\loadperf.dll” to side-jack the proper "loadperf.dll" file located in the "%WINDIR%\Windows\System32\" directory. A similar technique is used with the “winmm.dll” file when it is not in “%WINDIR%\System32\winmm.dll”. This technique has been used to launch HK Door, Crosswalk, and other malware.

actions.name: accessed compromised servers called hop points from numerous China-based IP addresses
actions.description: The cyber actors typically conducted their intrusions by accessing compromised servers called hop points from numerous China-based IP addresses resolving to different Chinese internet service providers (ISPs).

actions.name: used US-based and foreign-based email, social media, and other online accounts to develop online personas
actions.description: These cyber actors used US-based and foreign-based email, social media, and other online accounts to develop online personas in order to interact with the group, other conspirators, ISPs, web hosting providers, and victim companies.

actions.name: obtained use of servers by leasing remote access to them from hosting providers
actions.description: The actors obtained the use of servers, typically by leasing remote access to them, directly or indirectly from hosting providers.

actions.name: used leased servers to register and access operational email accounts, host command and control (C2) domains, and interact with victim networks
actions.description: They used these servers to register and access operational email accounts, host command and control (C2) domains, and interact with victim networks.

actions.name: used hop points as an obfuscation technique when interacting with victim networks
actions.description: The actors used these hop points as an obfuscation technique when interacting with victim networks.

actions.name: registered and used malicious domains that mimic prominent companies to deceive victims and cybersecurity systems
actions.description: The actors registered and used malicious domains that mimic prominent companies in order to deceive targeted victims, cybersecurity professionals, and cybersecurity systems into identifying Internet traffic associated with those domains as legitimate or benign.

actions.name: used socially engineered domains as command and control (C2) domains
actions.description: These socially engineered domain were usually used as C2 domains.

actions.name: created C2 dead drops (C2DD) by programming malware to contact accounts on publicly available web pages encoded with IP addresses of C2 servers
actions.description: These actors also created “C2 dead drops” (C2DD), whereby they programmed their malware to contact these C2DD accounts on publicly available web pages. The C2DD pages were encoded with the IP addresses of C2 servers.

actions.name: used encoded text strings with anchor text in C2DD pages to convert into actor-controlled IP addresses or C2 domains
actions.description: C2DD pages included what might appear to be random strings of text, with the relevant malware programmed to recognize the text strings—which typically started and/or ended with a pre-programmed “anchor text”—converting them into actor-controlled IP addresses or C2 domains.
